title: Praggnanandhaa and Caruana Set Up Generational Chess Clash in Grand Chess Tour Final
excerpt: India's 19-year-old prodigy dismantled Keymer 19-9 in the semifinal while the defending champion edged past Wesley So to reach Tuesday's championship match in St. Louis.
body:
• India's R. Praggnanandhaa and America's Fabiano Caruana will meet in the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals championship match on Tuesday in St. Louis, starting at 1 p.m. ET.
  • Praggnanandhaa demolished Germany's Vincent Keymer 19-9 in the semifinal, winning four consecutive games before the match was decided with four blitz games to spare.
  • Caruana, the defending champion and world number two, edged past Wesley So 18-12 in a tighter semifinal that hinged on rapid and blitz form.
  • The winner claims the Grand Chess Tour title and $200,000; the runner-up takes $125,000 from the $450,000 prize fund.

The 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals in St. Louis will culminate in a generational clash after 19-year-old Indian grandmaster R. Praggnanandhaa and 33-year-old American Fabiano Caruana advanced through their semifinal matches on Sunday to set up a championship showdown.

The final begins Tuesday, August 25, at 1 p.m. ET (10:30 p.m. IST) with the first of two classical games, followed by rapid and blitz sessions across the remaining days of the tournament.

Praggnanandhaa Overwhelms Keymer

Praggnanandhaa delivered the more emphatic semifinal performance, routing Germany's Vincent Keymer 19-9 in a match that was effectively over before the blitz games began. After blowing a winning position in the classical portion on Day 2, Keymer appeared unable to recover, losing three straight games to start Day 3.

https://x.com/ChessbaseIndia/status/2091652915815497912

"Yesterday must have been such a shock to the system that he's clearly not recovered."

— Peter Svidler, Grandmaster and commentator

Praggnanandhaa's first rapid game was what commentator IM Nazi Paikidze called his cleanest of the tournament. With Keymer already trailing by six points and opening with the Pirc Defense, the Indian traded queens on move five and ground out a one-sided endgame with what broadcast analysts described as machine-like accuracy.

In the second rapid, Keymer's 7.Nc3 allowed Praggnanandhaa a dream position in the Rossolimo Sicilian, and the German's queen was trapped by move 20. Though Keymer salvaged some pride by winning the final three blitz games, the match was decided well before that.

Caruana Holds Firm Against So

The other semifinal was a tighter contest. Caruana, the world number two and defending Grand Chess Tour champion, built a two-point lead after winning the bonus blitz game following two classical draws, then managed the advantage through two rapid games against Wesley So.

So's chances effectively ended in the first blitz game when a critical error on move 20 — Nd7 — cost him a pawn and the position collapsed. Caruana clinched the match 18-12 to advance to his second consecutive GCT Final.

A Rivalry With History

Tuesday's final pairs two players with a rich competitive history. Praggnanandhaa famously defeated Caruana in the 2023 FIDE World Cup semifinals en route to a final against Magnus Carlsen, and the two have traded results in speed chess events throughout 2025 and 2026.

"We've had some crazy matches in the past, so it's going to be interesting. It's going to be a close fight and who's going to show up at their best on a given day is going to take it."

— R. Praggnanandhaa

Caruana acknowledged the challenge: "It is clear he's a player who takes a lot of risks, and he'll give you chances, and he'll also punish you if you don't take those chances."

What's at Stake

The $450,000 tournament features a $200,000 top prize. A win would make Caruana the first player to claim back-to-back Grand Chess Tour titles. For Praggnanandhaa, it would be his maiden GCT championship — another milestone in a career that has already seen him become one of the youngest players to qualify for the Candidates tournament and reach a World Cup final.

Meanwhile, Keymer and So will contest the third-place match, with the winner earning a guaranteed spot in next year's Grand Chess Tour alongside salary-like compensation for the full season. The final runs through August 27.
